js_008: Almond is a novel by Sohn Won-pyung. A screenwriter and novelist, this is her signature work.
js_010: What is the name of the boy protagonist who can barely feel emotions?
js_015: The protagonist is Yunjae. He’s a sixteen-year-old boy who moves through the world without really feeling emotions.
js_017: What is the name of the condition Yunjae has, where he can’t recognize emotions well?
js_022: Yunjae has alexithymia. He rarely feels emotions like fear.
js_024: What brain organ tied to emotion does the title ‘Almond’ actually refer to?
js_029: ‘Almond’ refers to the amygdala. Shaped like an almond, this organ governs emotion, especially fear.
js_031: Compared to other people, what’s special about Yunjae’s amygdala?
js_034: He doesn’t have one at all
js_036: Yunjae’s amygdala is smaller, so emotional signals barely get through. That’s why he rarely feels fear or sadness.
js_038: What kind of shop does Yunjae’s mom run to make a living?
js_043: Mom runs a used bookstore to raise Yunjae. The shop is Yunjae’s whole world and a key setting in the story.
js_045: What affectionate nickname did Grandma use for Yunjae?
js_050: Grandma called Yunjae her pretty monster — a nickname that loves his difference exactly as it is, not as a flaw.
js_052: Which of Yunjae’s friends is a troublemaker who can’t control his anger?
js_057: Gon is a troublemaker who can’t rein in his emotions — the exact opposite of the emotionless Yunjae.
js_059: What tragic event happens to Grandma and Mom together?
js_060: A random knife attack by a stranger
js_064: On a day the family is together, a stranger commits a random knife attack. Grandma dies, and Mom is badly hurt.
js_066: What year was Almond first published by Changbi?
js_071: Almond came out from Changbi in 2017. It won the 10th Changbi Prize for Young Adult Literature and became a beloved bestseller.
js_078: Sohn Won-pyung, born in 1979, is a filmmaker and novelist. Almond won the Changbi Prize for Young Adult Literature and Japan’s Booksellers’ Award for translated fiction.
js_079: Yunjae is a boy who moves through life almost like an observer, barely feeling emotions. He’s the quiet narrator carrying the whole novel.
js_080: Alexithymia is a condition that makes it hard to recognize and express emotions. Yunjae especially struggles to feel fear and sadness.
js_081: ‘Almond’ refers to the amygdala in the brain. This small, almond-shaped organ handles fear and emotional responses.
js_082: Common mix-up — Yunjae’s amygdala isn’t large, it’s small. That’s the whole reason his emotional signals come through so faintly.
js_083: Mom’s used bookstore is Yunjae’s world and his refuge. It fits perfectly with his quiet, book-raised way of seeing things.
js_084: Grandma calls Yunjae her pretty monster. It’s the warmest love in the novel — embracing difference itself, not treating it as a flaw.
js_085: Gon is a troublemaker who can’t control his emotions. Standing opposite the emotionless Yunjae, their friendship becomes the heart of the story.
js_086: During a random knife attack on a day the family is together, Grandma dies and Mom is badly injured. It’s the event that flips Yunjae’s life upside down.
js_087: Published by Changbi in 2017, this is Sohn Won-pyung’s signature work. A young-adult coming-of-age novel beloved both at home and abroad.

js_102: The almond-shaped organ in the brain that governs emotion, especially fear. Yunjae’s is small, which is why he barely feels emotions — the root of the title.
js_103: Alexithymia — a condition that makes it hard to recognize and express emotion. It’s the trait that defines Yunjae’s quiet, flat way of seeing the world.
js_105: A boy who can’t feel emotions. He gets through the world by memorizing the ‘right’ reaction for each situation — the calm first-person narrator of the novel.
js_107: Mom runs a used bookstore and teaches Yunjae emotions one by one. Grandma calls him her pretty monster, loving him exactly as he is.
js_108: A troublemaker who can’t control his anger — an excess of emotion, the exact opposite of Yunjae’s lack of it. Their friendship is the heart of the story.
js_110: Fearless, emotionless Yunjae comforts the deeply wounded Gon without hesitation. Two ‘monsters’ — one lacking, one overflowing — end up saving each other.
js_112: What does it really mean to empathize with someone else’s pain? Through a child who feels nothing, the novel keeps circling back to this question.
js_114: The once-numb Yunjae collides with people, feels emotion for the first time, and finally grows into a person. The almond wakes up.
js_116: The Almond in My Head Is Quiet
js_117: The protagonist Yunjae has a small amygdala, so he barely feels emotions.
js_118: ‘Almond’ refers to the amygdala, the brain organ that governs emotion.
js_119: The story opens in the flat voice of a boy for whom both fear and sadness stay blurry.
js_120: Is a child with no emotions still a person? — the novel’s opening question.
js_123: Grandma calls Yunjae her pretty monster, loving him exactly as he is.
js_124: Mom runs a used bookstore and teaches Yunjae to memorize the right reaction for each situation.
js_125: Instead of real feelings, Yunjae gets by performing learned expressions.
js_126: The world’s stares and misunderstandings pile up around the emotionless boy.
js_128: That Day’s Attack — A World Collapses
js_129: On a day the family is together, a stranger commits a random knife attack.
js_130: Grandma dies, and Mom falls into a vegetative state.
js_131: Left alone, Yunjae survives on nothing but memorized reactions.
js_132: Dr. Shim, a family friend of Mom’s, stays by Yunjae’s side.
js_135: Gon, a troublemaker who’d gone missing, reappears in front of Yunjae.
js_136: Gon bullies Yunjae at first, but opens up to him because he shows no fear.
js_137: Dora, who loves running, teaches Yunjae what a crush feels like.
js_138: At Professor Yoon’s request, Yunjae poses as his son by his bedridden wife’s side.
js_139: Emotional lack (Yunjae) and excess (Gon) begin to reflect each other.
js_142: Chulsa, a thug fresh out of juvenile detention, drags Gon and Yunjae into danger.
js_143: In a dangerous confrontation, the moment comes when Yunjae might lose Gon.
js_144: Yunjae feels a burning emotion for the first time — the almond awakens.
js_145: Mom, who’d been in a vegetative state, wakes from her coma.
js_146: The boy who once felt nothing finally learns empathy and grows up.
js_147: Grandma calls the emotionless Yunjae her pretty monster and embraces him exactly as he is. She never tries to fix him — she loves the difference itself.
js_148: It makes you ask what it really means to love someone by accepting their difference as who they are, not as something broken.
js_150: At Professor Yoon’s request, Yunjae poses as his bedridden wife’s long-vanished son. A child with no emotions ends up comforting someone’s final moments.
js_151: It’s a paradox worth sitting with: even someone who can’t feel emotion can still comfort another person’s pain.
js_153: Beside a boy whose rage no one else could handle, the fearless Yunjae simply stays. His lack turns out to be what saves someone who’s hurting.
js_154: It makes you consider how what looks like a weakness can become someone else’s salvation.
js_155: Is someone who can’t feel emotions still a person?
js_156: Picture Yunjae getting through life on memorized reactions. The novel asks whether emotion is really all it takes to be human.
js_157: What does it actually mean to empathize with someone else’s pain?
js_158: Think about Yunjae staying fearlessly by Gon’s side. Empathy might not be only about feeling.
js_159: What really turns a person into a monster?
js_160: Set the emotionless Yunjae beside a world numb to violence, and ask who the real monster is.
